frameworks.name: Three Offer Differentiation Vectors
frameworks.definition: A commodity offer must win on at least one of three dimensions: speed (faster than competitors), risk-reduction (less risky than competitors), or ease (simpler experience for the customer). Focus on one vector and execute it well rather than mediocre coverage of all three.

frameworks.name: Three Lead Magnet Types
frameworks.definition: Lead magnets take one of three forms: (1) Reveal a Problem (e.g., '7 mistakes homeowners make'), (2) Trial of the Solution (give the core deliverable for free and follow up), or (3) One Step of Multi-Step (a splinter offer: give one component of the full offer for free or near-free, then upsell the rest).

frameworks.name: Attraction Offer Mechanisms
frameworks.definition: Four wrappings that convert an existing offer into a lead-generation vehicle without changing the core product: giveaway, win-your-money-back, decoy pricing, and buy-X-get-Y-free.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that commodity service businesses (e.g., home services such as roofing, kitchen remodeling, concrete) can escape price competition by winning on at least one of three value vectors: speed (deliver the outcome in one-third the time), risk reduction (insure or guarantee against the customer's biggest fear), or ease (reduce the friction in intake, onboarding, and pre-work). Winning on even one vector justifies a price premium that removes the business from commodity comparison.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Commodity or easily-compared service businesses (home services, contracting, etc.)
Markets where competitor comparison is easy and price pressure is high
claims.mechanism: When an offer delivers meaningfully faster, carries demonstrably less risk, or requires materially less customer effort, it exits the commodity comparison set and buyers will pay a premium rather than price-shop.
bounded_by: Does not require winning on all three vectors; one is sufficient if executed well

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that after deciding to differentiate on speed, the useful framing is not 'can we do this faster?' but 'what would it take to deliver this outcome in one-third the time?' Answering the second question (e.g., paying contractors 50% more for same-day responses) reveals whether the premium can be priced in and sold, rather than reflexively concluding it cannot be done.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founders in commodity service businesses with speed as the chosen differentiation vector
claims.mechanism: Reframing from a yes/no question to a cost-identification question forces the team to price the differentiation rather than dismiss it; if customers will pay the premium, the economics work.

numbers.axis: contractor cost premium to enable speed

bounded_by: If customers in the target segment do not value speed, the premium cannot be passed on; solution is to move up-market to wealthier customers who do

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that risk-reduction differentiation can be operationalized by purchasing an actual insurance policy against the customer's biggest fear and including its cost in the offer price, allowing the seller to honestly say 'we cover damages up to X, it's already included.' This is often cheaper than founders assume and creates a concrete, verifiable guarantee rather than a vague promise.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses where a specific customer fear (damage, non-completion) can be insured
Businesses with sufficient margin to absorb insurance premiums
claims.mechanism: An actual third-party insurance policy transforms a marketing promise ('we guarantee') into a contractual certainty ('we are insured against this'), reducing buyer skepticism and shifting risk perception.
bounded_by: Requires that the fear is specific and insurable; vague fears ('I won't like it') cannot be insured
Insurance premium must be below the incremental margin from the premium price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ease-of-experience differentiation is achieved by doing preparatory work for the customer before delivery begins: pre-intake data gathering, pre-onboarding steps, and pre-work that makes the customer's experience more seamless. Very few service businesses invest in this, so customers almost universally notice and appreciate it, creating a perception advantage disproportionate to the actual cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses where onboarding friction is a common customer complaint
Markets where competitors provide no pre-work or intake preparation
claims.mechanism: Pre-work reduces customer cognitive load and effort at the most uncertain moment (before results are visible), reducing friction-driven churn and increasing perceived value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that Acquisition.com's scaling roadmap lead magnet generates higher ROAS overall (measured across an extended time horizon) than direct-to-workshop ads, even though direct-to-workshop ads have higher immediate ROAS. The lead magnet also scales better because it reaches a broader segment of the awareness spectrum rather than only the warmest, most purchase-ready prospects.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with existing brand presence and the ability to run parallel ad campaigns
Offer structures with a free or low-friction front end (lead magnet) feeding a paid back-end (workshop)
claims.mechanism: Direct CTAs only reach the most-aware segments (small fraction of total market); lead magnets reach less-aware segments and convert them over time, producing more total buyers despite lower immediate conversion rates.

anchors.value: only the two most-aware segments (very small)

bounded_by: For businesses targeting only a small revenue goal, a direct CTA will produce higher immediate ROAS; the lead magnet advantage only materializes when scaling toward higher revenue tiers
Requires a back-end conversion process to capture the extended-horizon ROAS

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that 'request a quote' is one of the weakest possible calls to action for a home-services website because no customer wants to request a quote; they want a specific valuable outcome in exchange for their contact information. Replacing a quote request with a valuable, desire-matching lead magnet described in the customer's own language will materially improve lead volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Home services and local service businesses running Google Ads to a generic website
claims.mechanism: Customers are motivated by desire for an outcome, not by a process task (requesting quotes); a lead magnet offering a specific desirable outcome reduces the friction of information exchange.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a lead magnet framed around a specific, desirable outcome described in the customer's own language outperforms a generic request mechanism. His example of a strong lead magnet title format: '11 frameworks we use to build wildly profitable gyms' is more compelling than a vague category label because it names the dream outcome in the buyer's vocabulary.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2C and B2B lead generation with digital ads or content funnels
claims.mechanism: Language-matching the customer's existing internal narrative eliminates the translation work the prospect must do to determine relevance, lowering friction for opt-in.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that a 'trial of the solution' lead magnet, where one step of the core deliverable is given for free (and the customer is called back after experiencing value), is one of the highest-quality lead magnet formats because it generates high lead volume while creating a live demonstration of capability. He cites a business that gets local map rankings for free and calls back in seven days; this approach worked well for that company.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses where one discrete deliverable can be produced quickly and at low cost
Services where the initial result is immediately perceivable (e.g., map ranking, color palette assessment)
claims.mechanism: Delivering a slice of the real outcome removes skepticism more effectively than testimonials or demonstrations because the prospect personally experiences value before paying, lowering purchase risk perception.
bounded_by: Requires that the trial deliverable can be automated or done at low marginal cost
Not applicable when the full service requires the client's participation before any value can be generated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for a multi-step offer (A + B + C + D), extracting one component (e.g., component A) and giving it away for free or at deep discount, then positioning the remaining components (B + C + D) as the natural next step, is almost always possible and is often more powerful than selling the full bundle at once. The extracted component acts as a splinter offer that creates desire for the rest.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any offer with at least two distinct steps or components in the delivery process
Offers where one component can be delivered independently without requiring the others
claims.mechanism: Completing the first step creates both familiarity (the customer has experienced the provider) and a natural next-problem that the remaining components solve, reducing resistance at the point of upsell.
bounded_by: Requires that component A can be separated and delivered without components B, C, D
Not applicable when all components are so interdependent that partial delivery creates no standalone value

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that discounts should be large enough to change buyer behavior, targeting 80-90% off on a specific splinter component rather than 10-20% off the full price. Small discounts do not alter purchase decisions; only dramatic discounts shift behavior. The mechanism is to apply the steep discount to a component that has low delivery cost to maintain overall unit economics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses using discounting as a lead-generation tactic
Offers where a component of the full offer can be isolated and delivered cheaply
claims.mechanism: An 80-90% discount is psychologically category-shifting (it signals a fundamentally different product, not a negotiated concession), creating behavioral change rather than mild preference shift.

anchors.value: 10-20% off full price — does not change buyer behavior
80-90% off a low-cost splinter component — changes buyer behavior

bounded_by: The large discount must be applied to a component with low delivery cost; applying it to high-cost components destroys margin

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the best lead magnets are items that other people charge for — the more real the lead magnet (i.e., the more it has a genuine perceived market value or true cost to produce), the more likely it is to generate leads effectively.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any business using digital or content-based lead generation
claims.mechanism: When a lead magnet has observable market value (competitors charge for it), the offer signals real worth rather than a marketing incentive, reducing the prospect's skepticism about the free item being low quality.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a giveaway lead generation tactic, the highest-value use of runner-up contacts is to call all non-winners and offer them a discounted 'participation prize' (e.g., a $2,000 discount on kitchen remodeling), framing it as second place rather than a standard offer. This converts the loss into a positive frame while collecting a large warm lead pool from the giveaway.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses running prize giveaways as lead generation campaigns
Services with enough margin to offer a meaningful discount (e.g., $2,000 off)
claims.mechanism: Non-winners are warm (they entered because they wanted the service); reframing the discount as a prize rather than a sale removes the feeling of being pitched and preserves positive emotional state from the giveaway participation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in a Buy-X-Get-Y-Free structure, the total amount given away free must exceed the amount the customer pays; the price is then set to maintain unit economics while making the free portion feel like the more substantial part of the deal. Example structure: buy 4 months at $300 each ($1,200 total) and get 8 months free, rather than offering 12 months at $100 each.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Subscription or recurring-service businesses with discretion to restructure payment schedules
Businesses where multi-month or multi-unit bundles make sense
claims.mechanism: When the free component visibly exceeds the paid component in quantity, the buyer's reference point shifts to the total bundle value rather than the per-unit price, increasing perceived deal quality and conversion.

anchors.value: $300/month x 4 months = $1,200 — 8 free months, far more compelling

bounded_by: Requires checking local advertising law compliance; advertised discount structures vary by county and region

examples.text: Alex Hormozi described a company he met at an L3 event that built a lead generation business entirely on a trial-of-the-solution lead magnet. The company's service was getting local businesses ranked in positions 1, 2, or 3 in Google Maps local search results. Their lead magnet was: 'We will get you ranked 1, 2, or 3 for free, and then call you in seven days to see if you still want it.' According to Hormozi, this approach was working extremely well and generating a high volume of leads at low cost, because the prospect experienced the real deliverable before any purchase decision.

Alex Hormozi described a fashion consulting business (owner named Ashley) featured on a Cash Guys episode who was using a generic 'book a call for an assessment' offer — essentially a disguised request-a-quote. To create a stronger lead magnet, Hormozi recommended replacing it with an automated color palette assessment: prospects would get their color palette (what colors to wear based on skin tone, personality, etc.) for free, providing genuine value in exchange for contact information. The key was that this could be automated and delivered quickly, making the economics viable. Hormozi used this example to demonstrate how even a 'my service comes together as one whole' objection can be broken by identifying a small, separable piece of the process to give away.

Alex Hormozi described his own business running parallel ad campaigns: direct-to-workshop ads and scaling-roadmap lead-magnet ads. The direct-to-workshop ads had higher immediate ROAS because they targeted only people already ready to buy. The scaling roadmap had higher overall ROAS when measured across an extended time window and could scale further because it reached all awareness levels. Hormozi used this as a first-person example that even a large brand with proven authority cannot simply say 'give me money' and expect the same results as a softer, value-first lead magnet approach at scale.

practices.text: When your offer is in a commodity market, answer the question 'what would it take to deliver this outcome in one-third the time?' with your team before concluding it is not possible. The question forces cost-identification rather than reflexive rejection.

If improving speed requires paying contractors 50% more for same-day responsiveness, calculate whether customers will pay the premium before dismissing the approach. If current customers won't pay, move up-market to wealthier buyers who value speed, risk reduction, and ease.

For risk-reduction differentiation, get an actual insurance policy for the customer's biggest fear (damage, non-completion) and include it in the price. Include the cost in your offer rather than treating it as margin erosion.

Invest in pre-work and pre-onboarding details: knowing the customer's name and business before they arrive, preparing intake forms in advance, doing preparatory steps before the customer engages. These details are rare enough that customers consistently notice and appreciate them.

Replace 'request a quote' CTAs on home-services websites with a specific, desirable lead magnet described in the customer's own language. Give something the customer actually wants in exchange for their contact information.

For Buy-X-Get-Y-Free structures, set the free quantity above the paid quantity and price the paid units to recover full unit economics. Always verify with an attorney that the structure complies with local advertising laws before publishing.

When running a giveaway, call all non-winning entrants and offer them a discounted participation prize framed as 'second place' rather than as a standard sales call. The prize framing maintains positive affect from the giveaway and converts warm contacts.

To create a splinter offer, draw out your full offer components (A, B, C, D), take one component, and give it away at 80-90% off or free. Design the rest of your offer to be the natural next step after the customer experiences the splinter component.
For lead magnet design, give away something that other businesses charge for. The higher the true market value of the lead magnet, the more lead volume it generates.
